new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and falls on the syllable with a (phonetically) long vowel, which in this variety is the closed syllable; i.e. prominence tracks vowel length/closed-syllable weight rather than a fixed position. The companion Nagpuria sketch in the same volume (p. 459) says the same thing the other way round: syllables with long vocoids are always stressed, and length is predictable (monosyllables long; second syllable long in longer words).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a phoneme-inventory sketch of Jharkhand Sadan/Sadri (sadr1248); no data on phrases or citation forms. Applies to Bangladesh Oraon Sadri (orao1237) only by extension; no source describes Oraon Sadri phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: No phonological or grammatical description of Oraon Sadri (orao1237, the Sadri of the Oraon/Kurukh diaspora in NW Bangladesh; Glottolog 5.1 lists 0 descriptive refs, OLAC lists only Glottolog and Ethnologue) could be found. The stress statement quoted below is a PROXY: it describes Sadan/Sadri of Jharkhand = Sadri [sck] sadr1248 (LSI Jharkhand 2023), the parent variety from which Bangladesh Oraon Sadri descends; Glottolog/Ethnologue split sdr from sck on the basis of unpublished SIL Bangladesh survey data, not on any published phonology. The same volume's Nagpuria chapter (also sadr1248) gives a compatible statement (p. 459: syllables with long vocoids are always stressed). Das & Raha 1963 (the one Glottolog ref with a language chapter, on Sunderban Oraons in West Bengal) describes their Sadri as a Hindi-Bengali mixture with sample texts only; no phonology. Reviewer must decide whether a sister-code source is admissible for orao1237; I have not marked it a catalog candidate.

new_statements.quote: p. 222: "In Sadri, it is found that each word has one main stress indicated by the symbol [ ' ]. From the research, it is found that words consisting of a single syllable bearing this main accent. On the other hand, the secondary accent is indicated by the symbol [ ` ]. It varies considerably. In the case of isolated verb forms consisting of two syllables, the main accent always lies on the second syllable." [examples p. 223, accents as printed: /naraj/ [nàráj] 'angry', /mesa/ [mèsá] 'mix', /ulʈa/ [ùlʈá] 'opposite', /kəɖa/ [kə̀ṛá] 'dig out'; /məhina/ [məhìná] 'month', /beiman/ [bə́imàn] 'cheat', /ilekson/ [íleksòn] 'election'; p. 225-226: /paisa/ [páisà] 'money', /dimag/ [dìmág] 'brain', /raja/ [ràjá] 'king', /jamun/ [jámùn] 'berry', /patai/ [pàtái] 'leaf'] p. 226: "From the above examples, it is clear that Sadri has two prominant word-accents namely primary and secondary. In monosyllabic words, only the primary word accent is seen and in two syllabic words, both primary and secondary word accents have been seen. On the other hand, words with three and more syllables have also two accents and here, other syllables remain unaccented. It is also seen that in multi-syllabic words with complex peak i.e. with diphthongs, main accent is remained on the syllable with complex peak."

new_statements.relation_note: PROXY (Assam tea-garden Sadri = sadr1248, not Bangladesh Oraon Sadri). No catalog record for orao1237. Against the one statement held by the project (Ghosh & Pattanaik 2023 LSI Jharkhand Sadan/Sadri: stress non-phonemic, 'mainly with long vowels in the close syllable', read weight-sensitive) Saikia is compatible in type (non-contrastive, heavy nucleus attracts the main accent) and adds detail: default second/final-syllable primary accent in disyllables, diphthong attraction in polysyllables, one secondary accent per word; the weight criterion differs in wording (diphthongs rather than long vowels in closed syllables).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Every word carries one primary accent (monosyllables carry it alone); polysyllables carry one primary and one secondary accent, remaining syllables unaccented. Stated rules: in disyllabic verb forms in isolation the primary accent is always on the second syllable; in polysyllables containing a diphthong ('complex peak') the primary accent sits on the diphthong syllable. The transcribed examples (pp. 223-226) show the primary accent mostly on the final syllable of di- and trisyllables without diphthongs ([nàráj], [ràjá], [pàháṛ], [dìmág], [jərúr], [məhìná], [tetèŋá], [bʰarùwá]) and on the diphthong syllable where there is one ([bə́imàn], [páisà], [pʰə́isəlà], [báundarì], [brìhəspáit], [satànəbbói]), with a residue of initial-accented words the author does not explain ([jámùn], [níyə̀m], [ghúŋgì], [ánùsər], [íleksòn], [ádʰuniktà], [janówàr]). No claim that accent is contrastive; no minimal pairs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: one secondary accent [ ` ] per polysyllabic word, position 'varies considerably' (p. 222); in the examples it usually falls on the first syllable when the primary is final ([nàráj], [bìsakʰápətnəm]) and on a later syllable when the primary is initial ([íleksòn], [páildʰà])
new_statements.exceptions: none stated as such; the example lists contain initial-accented words without diphthongs ([jámùn] 'berry', [níyə̀m] 'rules', [ánùsər] 'according to', [íleksòn] 'election', [ádʰuniktà] 'modernity') that the two stated rules do not cover
new_statements.identity_note: orao1237 is Oraon Sadri (ISO sdr), the Sadri spoken by Oraon/Kurux communities in Bangladesh. Saikia 2015 describes the Sadri of Assam tea-garden communities (Assam University, Silchar); Kiran & Peterson 2011 describe Sadri/Nagpuri of central-western Jharkhand (Chotanagpur) as lingua franca, phonology after Jordan-Horstmann 1969; Srivastava 1989 describes Nagpuriya of Ranchi district (then Bihar). All three are sadr1248 varieties and serve only as proxies for orao1237.

new_statements.quote: p. 61: "The length is not phonemic. However, the long vocoids occur in the phonetic level and their occurrences are predictable. The vocoids occurring in the mono-syllabic words are uniformly long; while in di-syllabic, tri-syllabic and tetra-syllabic words (available a very few), the vocoids of the second syllable are long. Stress also is a co-occurring feature with the length, i.e., the syllables having long vocoids are always stressed." p. 48: "In Nagpuriya, there are thirty six (36) phonemes, out of which thirty five (35) are segmental phonemes and one (1) is suprasegmental phoneme." [i] occurs elsewhere."

new_statements.relation_note: PROXY (Ranchi Nagpuriya = sadr1248, by the same S.P. Srivastava who co-wrote the LSI Jharkhand 'Nagpuria' sketch held by the project). No catalog record for orao1237. Against the statement held by the project (LSI Jharkhand 2023 Sadan/Sadri: stress non-phonemic, phonetic length 'predictable only in the close syllable', stress 'mainly with long vowels in the close syllable' = weight-sensitive) Srivastava agrees that stress is non-phonemic and rides on predictable phonetic length, but states a different conditioning: length (and stress) go to the SECOND syllable of any polysyllable, open or closed ([papi:ta], [bani:]), i.e. a positional (fixed: second syllable) rule rather than a closed-sylla…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not a phoneme (the only suprasegmental phoneme is nasalisation). Vowel length is non-phonemic and positionally predictable: vowels of monosyllables are long, and in words of two to four syllables the vowel of the second syllable is long; stress always accompanies the long vowel. Hence: monosyllables stressed; polysyllables stressed on the second syllable (= the final syllable in the disyllables that dominate the lexicon), e.g. [bani:] 'saying', [papi:ta] 'papaya', [kata:ri] 'sugarcane'.
new_statements.exceptions: none; tetra-syllabic words said to be very few
new_statements.identity_note: orao1237 is Oraon Sadri (ISO sdr), the Sadri spoken by Oraon/Kurux communities in Bangladesh. Saikia 2015 describes the Sadri of Assam tea-garden communities (Assam University, Silchar); Kiran & Peterson 2011 describe Sadri/Nagpuri of central-western Jharkhand (Chotanagpur) as lingua franca, phonology after Jordan-Horstmann 1969; Srivastava 1989 describes Nagpuriya of Ranchi district (then Bihar). All three are sadr1248 varieties and serve only as proxies for orao1237.

readall_conflicts: No catalog record exists for orao1237 and none of the three works describes Bangladesh Oraon Sadri; all are proxies for Indian Sadri/Nagpuri (sadr1248), like the LSI Jharkhand statement already held by the project. Among the proxies: Kiran & Peterson 2011 is silent on stress (length non-phonological only). Saikia 2015 (Assam Sadri) and the LSI 2023 statement agree in type (non-contrastive accent drawn to a heavy nucleus) but word the weight criterion differently (diphthong syllable vs. long vowel in a closed syllable), and Saikia adds a default second/final-syllable primary accent for disyllabic verbs plus one secondary accent per word, with several unexplained initial-accented examples. Srivastava 1989 (Ranchi Nagpuriya) states a positional rule instead: non-phonemic length and stress fall on the second syllable of every polysyllable (open or closed) and on monosyllables, which reads fixed: second syllable, not weight-sensitive; it coincides with the others for CVCVC disyllables but not for words like [papi:ta] (open second syllable long/stressed) or for Saikia's final-accented trisyllables ([məhìná]).
